theme.title: Was wollen wir trinken (Sieben Tage lang)
theme.variety: standard German, sung, with a few spoken short forms

title: What shall we drink, seven days long (Sieben Tage lang)
summary: The pub and protest singalong: drink together, work together, strike together. Easy words, lots of repetition, and your first look at wollen and müssen.
goals: Sing the chorus: Was wollen wir trinken, sieben Tage lang?
Understand wollen and müssen with a second verb at the end
Learn the solidarity words: zusammen, nicht allein, keiner kämpft allein
Hear spoken short forms: roll', fass' an

sections.title: About this song
sections.text:
The melody is older than all the words: it is **Son ar chistr**, a Breton song written in 1929 by two teenagers from Morbihan. Alan Stivell made it famous in 1970. In 1976 the Dutch band **Bots** wrote new words for it, 'Zeven dagen lang', and in 1980 they recorded this German version, **Sieben Tage lang**, also known by its first line, 'Was wollen wir trinken'.

The words you sent are that version: first drinking, then working, then striking together. That's why it's sung in pubs and at folk sessions, and also at demonstrations. The video link is an upload by a channel called DSC.

Why it's good for you: almost every line comes twice, the words are short, and it shows **wollen** and **müssen**, which come in Unit 3.

sections.title: wollen and müssen: the second verb goes to the end
sections.text:
- [[Was wollen wir trinken?]] [[wollen]] = to want. [[Was wollen wir ...?]] is a friendly way to say 'What shall we ...?'. The second verb, [[trinken]], goes to the **end**.
- [[Jetzt müssen wir streiken]]. [[müssen]] = to have to, must. Same pattern: [[müssen]] in second place, [[streiken]] at the end.
- You'll learn this properly in Unit 3 (können, wollen, müssen + verb bracket). For now, sing it and notice the shape: verb 1 ... verb 2 at the end.

Armenian puts the verb at the end too, so the 'bracket' will feel natural to you.

items.de: Es wird genug für alle sein!
items.note: genug = enough; für alle = for everyone

items.de: Wir halten zusammen, keiner kämpft allein
items.en: We stick together, nobody fights alone
items.note: zusammenhalten = to stick together; keiner = nobody

items.de: Dann wollen wir schaffen, komm fass' an!
items.en: Then let's work, come on, lend a hand!
items.note: schaffen = to work (southern Germany); fass' an = fass an, from anfassen: grab hold

items.de: Jetzt müssen wir streiken, keiner weiß, wie lang
items.en: Now we have to strike, nobody knows how long
items.note: wie lang = how long (often wie lange)

items.de: Dann kriegt der Frust uns nicht mehr klein
items.en: Then frustration won't wear us down any more
items.note: jemanden kleinkriegen = to wear someone down (colloquial); kriegen = bekommen

sections.title: Words worth a second look
sections.text:
- [[schaffen]]: in the south (Bavaria, Swabia) it means **to work**: [[Ich muss schaffen.]] = I have to work. Everywhere else it means **to manage, to get done**: [[Das schaffe ich!]] = I can do it! Both are useful in Munich.
- [[roll' das Fass mal rein]] and [[komm fass' an]]: the apostrophe marks a dropped -e, like [[ich sitz]] in 'Barfuß am Klavier'. [[mal]] softens the order: 'just roll it in'.
- [[streiken]]: strikes (Streiks) are a normal part of German life. You'll see [[Streik]] on train and airport boards when trains don't run.
- [[kriegen]] is the everyday spoken word for [[bekommen]] (to get): [[Ich kriege einen Kaffee.]]

sections.title: How to use it
sections.text:
1. Listen once with the link above.
2. Open the full lyrics and sing along: every line comes twice, so the second time you can join in.
3. The best practice is a real pub: in Munich, folk and Irish pubs still sing this. Now you know the words.

items.question: In Munich, a colleague says 'Ich muss heute lange schaffen.' What does schaffen mean here?
items.explanation: In southern Germany schaffen means to work (arbeiten). Elsewhere it means to manage: Das schaffe ich!

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: Now we have to strike.
items.explanation: müssen = to have to; wir müssen. The second verb (streiken) goes to the end.
